title: Describing people and places, and comparing them
goal: Describe people and places with adjectives that take the right endings, then compare two things — and recognize the ten adjectives whose comparative forms have to be memorized.
bekal: using adjectives with endings that match the gender, number and case of the noun
forming comparatives with *-iji / -ji / -ši* and superlatives with *naj-*
saying "more … than" with *od* + genitive or with *nego*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kakvo je Sarajevo?
dialogs.intro: Afternoon coffee, and Amina finally asks the question she's been holding back since Budi's first day.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Budi, kakvo je Sarajevo u poređenju s Jakartom?
lines.id: Budi, what's Sarajevo like compared to Jakarta?
lines.literal: Budi, what-like-n it-is Sarajevo in comparison-loc with Jakarta-ins?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Mnogo manje! Jakarta je ogromna — deset miliona ljudi.
lines.id: Much smaller! Jakarta is huge — ten million people.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Deset miliona? Sarajevo ima tri stotine hiljada.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Zato je ovdje mirnije. I zrak je čistiji… ljeti.

lines.text: Zimi nije. Zimi je zrak ovdje među najgorima u Evropi.

lines.text: Znam, rekli su mi. A koji je grad ljepši — Sarajevo ili Mostar?

lines.text: Mostar je topliji i stariji, ali Sarajevo je moje.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: A kakav je tvoj novi komšija?

lines.literal: and what-like-m he-is your-m new-m neighbor?

lines.text: Visok, mršav, sijeda kosa. Vrlo tih, ali ljubazan.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Osamdeset dvije. I još se penje stepenicama brže od mene.
lines.id: Eighty-two. And he still climbs the stairs faster than me.

notes: ***Kakav?* asks about qualities, *koji?* asks for a choice.** *Kakav je tvoj komšija?* = what's he like? *Koji je tvoj komšija?* = which one is your neighbor? Both change their endings to match the noun: *kakav grad, kakva kuća, kakvo Sarajevo*.

***Sarajevo je moje*** — *moje*, not *moj*, because *Sarajevo* is neuter. City names in Bosnian have gender like any other noun: *Sarajevo* and *Mostar* are different genders, and it shows in the adjective.

***Brže od mene* — "faster than me".** There are two ways to say "than": *od* + genitive (*od mene, od Mostara*) or *nego* + the ordinary form (*nego ja, nego Mostar*). Both are equally correct and equally common; the first is a little shorter.

***Među najgorima* is the instrumental plural of a superlative** — exactly the *-ima* ending you learned in Unit 16. There's no new rule here; comparative adjectives follow the cases just like ordinary adjectives.

**Sarajevo's air in winter.** The city sits in a narrow valley, and when cold air traps the smoke from wood and coal stoves at the bottom of the valley (*inverzija*), its air quality is among the worst in Europe for a few weeks. Words you'll hear on the news: *smog*, *inverzija*, *zagađenje* (pollution). The rest of the year the air is actually clean — Budi isn't wrong, he just hasn't lived through a January yet.

grammars.title: Adjectives — position and agreement
body: Bosnian adjectives agree with their noun in three ways at once: gender, number and case. The good news is that the endings are almost the same as those of the demonstrative *ovaj / ova / ovo* you learned in Unit 3.
after: **Adjectives go before the noun**, just as in English: *lijep grad* (a beautiful city), *stara kuća* (an old house), *novo pismo* (a new letter). After *biti* they still agree in gender: *Grad je lijep. Kuća je stara.*

**The masculine has two shapes, and the difference is subtle.** *Dobar* (short) is used when the adjective gives new information or stands after *biti*: *On je dobar čovjek.* *Dobri* (long) is used when the thing is already known: *Gdje je onaj dobri konobar?* At A1 the two are almost interchangeable without anyone misunderstanding — your ear will pick the right one by itself later.

**When several adjectives come together, they all agree:** *jedna mala stara bosanska kuća*. That's what makes Bosnian sentences look long on the page, even though only one letter changes in each word.

**Adjectives are often made from nouns with the endings *-ski*, *-ni*, *-ov*:** *Bosna → bosanski*, *grad → gradski*, *voz → vozni*, *brat → bratov*. Once you recognize these endings, you can guess the meaning of many adjectives you've never seen.

grammars.title: More and most
body: Comparatives are formed with three endings, and superlatives always with the prefix *naj-*. The ten most common adjectives are the irregular ones — and those are exactly the ones you need to learn.
after: **The most common ending is *-iji***: *star → stariji*, *pametan → pametniji*, *hladan → hladniji*. If you don't know an adjective's comparative, using *-iji* will almost always be understood — and is often right.

***Naj-* goes in front of the comparative, with no exceptions**: *bolji → najbolji*, *veći → najveći*, *ljepši → najljepši*. It's written as one word, and the *j* is never dropped even when the base word already starts with *j*: *najjeftiniji*, with two *j*s.

**"Than" has two forms, both correct:** *Sarajevo je manje **od** Jakarte* (with the genitive) or *Sarajevo je manje **nego** Jakarta* (with the ordinary form). For equality: *Mostar je isto tako lijep **kao** Sarajevo* (just as beautiful as).

**Adverbs follow the same rule, irregulars included:** *brzo → brže* (fast), *dobro → bolje* (well), *loše → gore* (badly), *mnogo → više* (much), *malo → manje* (little). Everyday sentences that use them: *Možete li govoriti sporije?* (could you speak more slowly?) and *Bolje mi je* (I'm feeling better).

sections.title: Kakav je? — the most common adjectives

blocks.text: Adjectives are easiest to learn in pairs of opposites. All are given in the masculine form; for feminine add *-a*, for neuter *-o*.

head: Describing people
English
rows: He has blond / brown / gray hair.
He looks younger than he is.

blocks.title: Three intensifiers that change a sentence's tone
items: ***Vrlo*** and ***jako*** both mean "very", but *jako* sounds livelier and is far more common in conversation: *jako lijepo, jako hladno, jako mi se sviđa*. *Vrlo* is a bit more written.
***Malo*** means "a little" and is used to soften: *malo umoran* (a bit tired), *malo skupo* (a bit pricey). Bosnians use it all the time to avoid sounding too blunt.

***Pre-*** goes in front of an adjective to mean "too": *preskupo* (too expensive), *prehladno* (too cold), *prelijepo* (stunning — here it's actually praise). If you're bargaining at the market, the single word *preskupo* is enough to start the conversation.
